summary: Specifies Bump-in-the-API (BIA), a way for dual stack hosts to let existing IPv4-only applications talk to IPv6 hosts. It translates between the IPv4 and IPv6 socket APIs rather than translating IP headers. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 6535.

eli5.summary: An old program only speaks one language. BIA puts a translator between the program and the network so it can chat with newer machines without being rewritten.

questions: what is bump in the api
how can ipv4 applications talk to ipv6 hosts
how can ipv4 applications use ipv6
subtitle: Let old IPv4 applications talk to IPv6 servers without rewriting them.

tldr.problem: During the transition from IPv4 to IPv6, many existing applications were written to use only IPv4 network APIs and cannot speak to IPv6 servers without being rewritten.
tldr.mechanism: Bump-in-the-API (BIA) inserts a translator between an application's socket API calls and the TCP/IP stack. It intercepts IPv4 API calls from the application, translates them to IPv6 API calls, communicates with IPv6 hosts, and translates replies back to IPv4 format.
tldr.outcome: BIA allows IPv4-only applications to work on dual-stack hosts without modification, but does not work well for applications that hardcode IP addresses in data. It was an experimental approach that was superseded by RFC 6535.

facts.value: Dual-stack hosts with both IPv4 and IPv6 stacks

facts.value: Cannot translate embedded IP addresses in application data

today: RFC 3338 is Experimental and was superseded by RFC 6535. BIA was an approach useful for early adopters during IPv6 transition, but modern practice is to port applications to native IPv6 support rather than using translation mechanisms.

sections.title: The Dual Stack Problem
sections.content:
During the transition from IPv4 to IPv6, many existing applications were built to use only IPv4 socket APIs and cannot communicate with IPv6 addresses. At the same time, deploying both IPv4 and IPv6 on the same host (dual stack) became necessary. The challenge was: how can old IPv4 applications run on dual-stack hosts and reach IPv6 servers?

Previous approaches like Bump-in-the-Stack (RFC 2767) translated IP headers at the network layer, but that approach required driver modifications and could not be easily implemented on all systems. RFC 3338 proposes a solution called Bump-in-the-API that works at the socket API level instead, avoiding IP header translation altogether.
sections.eli5: When IPv6 was being adopted, old programs still only knew how to speak IPv4. The challenge was making these programs work with IPv6 servers without completely rewriting them.

sections.title: The BIA Architecture
sections.content:
BIA places an API translator layer between the socket API and the TCP/IP stack on a dual-stack host. The translator has three main components. The Function Mapper intercepts IPv4 socket function calls from the application and translates them to equivalent IPv6 function calls, and vice versa. The Name Resolver intercepts name lookups (like gethostbyname()), queries for both A (IPv4) and AAAA (IPv6) records, and returns synthesized IPv4 addresses for discovered IPv6 hosts. The Address Mapper maintains an internal table mapping the synthesized IPv4 addresses to real IPv6 addresses.

When an IPv4 application wants to reach an IPv6 host, the name resolver gets the IPv6 address, assigns a temporary IPv4 address from a reserved pool (like 0.0.0.1 through 0.0.0.255), and returns that fake IPv4 address. When the application makes API calls using this address, the function mapper translates them to IPv6 API calls.
sections.eli5: BIA has three helpers: one translates function calls, one handles name lookups and hands out fake IPv4 addresses that secretly map to IPv6 addresses, and one keeps track of the mapping.

sections.title: How Communication Works
sections.content:
When an IPv4 application on a BIA host needs to connect to a remote server, it first looks up the server's name. The name resolver intercepts this request and queries the DNS for both A and AAAA records. If only an AAAA record exists (the server is IPv6-only), the address mapper assigns a fake IPv4 address from the reserved pool and creates a mapping entry. The name resolver then returns this fake IPv4 address to the application.

When the application makes socket API calls with this fake IPv4 address, the function mapper detects them, looks up the real IPv6 address in the mapping table, and invokes the corresponding IPv6 socket API functions instead. Replies from the IPv6 host are translated back to IPv4 format for the application.

The reverse happens when an IPv6 host initiates communication to a BIA host: incoming IPv6 connections are translated to IPv4 socket calls for the local IPv4 applications.
sections.eli5: When a program asks for the server, BIA secretly gives it a fake IPv4 address that actually maps to the real IPv6 address. When the program makes a network call, BIA translates it to IPv6 and talks to the server, then translates the reply back.

sections.title: Limitations and Challenges
sections.content:
BIA works well for applications that use socket APIs normally, but has important limitations. Applications that embed IP addresses inside their data (like FTP, which sends IP addresses in the data part of messages) cannot be handled correctly by socket-level translation alone. IPv4 applications also cannot use IPv6's advanced features, and IPv6 applications cannot use all their advanced features when communicating with IPv4 applications.

The address mapping pool is limited, so many simultaneous IPv6 connections can exhaust available addresses. Additionally, when a dual-stack server has both IPv4 and IPv6 services on different ports, clients using BIA might fail if they expect IPv4 but get an IPv6 address.

The RFC recommends BIA only for early adopters with a few IPv4 applications, not for production use. Application developers should port their code to IPv6 instead of relying on BIA.
sections.eli5: BIA doesn't work for programs that hide IP addresses inside messages (like when sending a file transfer). The fake address pool can run out, and some advanced network features don't translate well.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
BIA operates at the API level rather than the IP header level, which provides some security advantages over NAT-PT. Applications can use network security features like IPsec when communicating with IPv6 hosts via BIA. The RFC notes that BIA does not require a DNS Application Layer Gateway like NAT-PT does, so it does not interfere with DNSSEC.

However, address pooling can create denial-of-service vulnerabilities if attackers can exhaust the available address space. BIA implementations should employ the same protection techniques as NAT-PT to mitigate these risks.
sections.eli5: BIA is safer in some ways than other translation methods because it works at a higher level. But attackers could still use up all the fake addresses on purpose.
